title: Optical switching of magnetic order in few-layer CrSBr
authors: Lukas Husel, Julian Trapp, Moritz Würf, Anna Rupp, Tim Wedl, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Iva Plutnarova, Zdenek Sofer, Alexander Högele
abstract: Manipulating magnetism with light is crucial for both fundamental understanding and technological advancements of information storage devices. The layered antiferromagnet CrSBr, part of the recently emerging class of two-dimensional van der Waals magnets, offers a unique path towards optical control of magnetism via magneto-excitons, which allow optical readout of the spin alignment and also provide a strong absorption channel. Here, we use exciton absorption and photoluminescence to demonstrate optical switching of the magnetic order in bi- and trilayer CrSBr. Using a continuous-wave laser with a power as low as a few microwatts at near-critical external magnetic fields, we demonstrate both local and remote switching of the magnetic configuration in extended lateral domains and further employ this mechanism to deterministically prepare the zero-field magnetic configuration. Our results establish optical switching as a useful means of controlling magnetism in CrSBr, with potential applications in magneto-optoelectronic devices.
summary: The authors demonstrate that the magnetic order in few-layer CrSBr can be switched using low-power optical excitation. By monitoring exciton energies and photoluminescence, they show that light can induce spin-flip transitions across extended areas, enabling deterministic control over the material's magnetic ground state. This establishes a promising platform for next-generation magneto-optoelectronic devices.
main_problem: The study aims to demonstrate and utilize optical switching of magnetic order in few-layer CrSBr, a 2D van der Waals magnet.
main_result: Low-power continuous-wave laser excitation can induce spin-flip transitions ($	ext{AFM} 	o 	ext{FM}$) in the bilayer, and remote switching was observed across extended domains. The critical field for certain transitions decreases significantly with increasing laser power.
method: The researchers used exciton absorption and photoluminescence spectroscopy with a continuous-wave laser to probe magnetic state changes as a function of applied magnetic field and laser power.
model_or_system: The physical system is few-layer CrSBr, an antiferromagnetic 2D van der Waals magnet encapsulated by hBN. The magnetism can be controlled via magneto-excitons, which provide both optical readout and strong absorption channels for energy transfer.
key_observables: Exciton energies ($	ext{XA}$, $	ext{XB}$), magnetic configuration (AFM, FM, MS, AFMB), critical switching power ($P_{	ext{crit}}$), and critical magnetic fields ($B_{	ext{crit}}$).
important_parameters: Laser power as low as a few microwatts ($\mu	ext{W}$); near-critical external magnetic fields; temperature (cryogenic conditions).
main_assumptions: The switching mechanism is attributed to energy transfer via exciton absorption coupling to the spin lattice, excluding substrate heating or photo-doping effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate exciton signatures confirming magnetic transitions under varying B fields; PL evolution maps demonstrate $	ext{AFM} 	o 	ext{FM}$ switching upon increasing laser power and observing local/remote switching patterns.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents measurements using DR and PL spectroscopy, first establishing the dependence of exciton energies on magnetic order (Fig. 1), then demonstrating optical control by varying laser power (Fig. 2), and finally mapping out the complex interplay between applied fields and optical power to deterministically set the zero-field state (Fig. 3, Fig. 5).
why_interesting: This work provides a direct experimental demonstration of optically controlling magnetic states in a solid-state material using light-matter coupling via excitons, which is highly relevant for developing quantum or magneto-optoelectronic devices.
